beats.got: Try several checkers and pick the best one. Fine, but it's a method, not an idea.

beats.got: Homework before the session. I would skip it. The calendar is full.

beats.trigger: ## Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: There is truth out there.
beats.got: The model makes things up in the same tone as when it's right. I knew that. 'Grounded' just means it can be traced to a source.

beats.trigger: Ten unverified steps in a row (retrieval, synthesis, formatting, writing, checking, rewriting, summarising, publishing) at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end
beats.got: Small error rates compound across a chain of steps. I can check that arithmetic myself, and it explains why the pilots looked fine and the workflows didn't.

beats.trigger: Say the detector catches 90% of them.
beats.got: The 0.01% figure rests on an assumed 90% catch rate. That's the whole question, and the slide assumes it.

beats.trigger: Later models may fabricate less; the mechanism stays the same.
beats.got: Asking the model to check itself doesn't count as a check. It also admits the problem may shrink.

beats.trigger: You catch some things, miss others, and never know what you missed.
beats.got: Don't trust advice about which method works. Measure on your own material. That's ordinary engineering, and fair.

beats.trigger: Four candidates that fail in different directions, so the scoreboard shows real spread:
beats.got: Four checks, each catching a different kind of error: invention, overreach, fake citations, contradicted claims. A clear taxonomy.

beats.trigger: Citation integrity caught a quote absent from the linked sanctions order.
beats.got: A real court case, and a checker that found a quote missing from the source document. That's concrete and I could verify it myself.

beats.trigger: A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The checker documents its own blind spots. Candour about limits is what I look for.

beats.trigger: A check makes your standard repeatable.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: Two runs prove nothing, and the slide says so. No hype, which I respect.

beats.trigger: The winner becomes a judge file you carry into Module 6.
beats.got: Fifty-five minutes, and I end up with a reusable checker file. Fine, I'll run it.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: We deliberately make the AI write a flawed briefing so the checkers have something to find. Odd, but it gives a known answer to test against.

beats.trigger: Why a separate worker? It runs in its own context, so your main session never sees what was fabricated.
beats.got: I don't look at the answer before the test, so I can't bias it. Same as a blind test.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.
beats.got: The agent breaks the briefing into 30 checkable claims. They admit the sample is too small to prove anything.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.
beats.got: Four agents work in parallel while I watch. Nothing for me to do. Quite efficient.

beats.trigger: A fifth agent (the scorer) reads the claim pool and all four detector files, adjudicates the 30 claims, and produces a scoreboard.
beats.got: Another AI grades the checkers. The scorer is also an LLM, so who checks it? Nobody explains that yet.

beats.trigger: You can point at a row and say *this is why I'm keeping this one*.
beats.got: A table showing which checker caught what on my own material. It's something I can test myself instead of believing someone's claim. This is the first real difference from the last three programmes.

beats.trigger: The "known limit" line names what you measured and decided not to chase.
beats.got: I end up with a saved checker file that states what it misses. A usable artefact, not a slide.

beats.trigger: Your benchmark had 30 claims. A production judge wants hundreds.
beats.got: This was a small demo, and real use needs ten times the effort. Honest.

beats.trigger: The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.
beats.got: The pattern is general: try candidates, measure, keep the winner. Sensible but obvious once stated.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the benchmark and updates the root instructions file with rules for when future sessions run a groundedness check before trusting an output.
beats.got: The agent writes rules for itself about when to run the check next time. Plausible, a bit procedural.

beats.trigger: The agent's report describes what it intended, not what is in the file.
beats.got: Don't trust the agent's report. Open the file and check what's there. Fair point, and a candid one.

beats.trigger: Push back where it's wrong
beats.got: Argue with the summary if it's vague. Sure.

beats.trigger: Propose, double-check, apply.
beats.got: The agent proposes, a check runs, then it acts. Sounds like a normal approval process.

beats.trigger: Ask which rung this action has earned.
beats.got: More reading, plus a ladder metaphor. Sounds like a maturity model. We have seen those.

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a source; accurate is harder.
beats.got: Traceable to a source is not the same as true. The first bullet already says that.

beats.trigger: Ethan Mollick, "Garbage Can and Bitter Lesson."
beats.got: More homework.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build, and feed its feedback into generation between rounds.
beats.got: The next step is the same thing at scale, run automatically. Sensible and not hyped.

take_homes: Chaining unchecked AI steps compounds errors. 85% per step over ten steps is about 20% end to end. I can check that arithmetic myself.
Don't believe advice on which checking method works. Run a few on your own material and read the scoreboard.
A good checker states what it can't catch, and a small benchmark of 30 claims is a demo, not proof.

monday.move: Probably nothing. If I get a spare hour, I'd take one briefing a team has already written from AI, extract about 30 claims and run two of the checks to see whether the scoreboard shows anything.
monday.who: Me, with one analyst from my team
monday.when: Not before the current programme's steering groups are done, probably in two to three weeks
monday.stop_condition: If the checks flag nothing real on the first briefing, or I can't tell who verifies the scorer, I drop it
monday.blocker: My calendar and my scepticism. Also unclear who owns the scorer and whether customer data can go into the tool, which our legal team will ask about.

misconception.why: Wait-and-see is still reasonable for the big claims. But here I could test the thing myself and see a result on my own material, with limits stated openly. That is different from agile, digital and OKRs, though the evidence is one small demo and the scorer is itself an LLM.

one_line: First one of these where I could test the claim myself, and it admits thirty claims proves nothing, but it's still homework-heavy and half the slides could go.
